title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
snippet: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A different thing that could happen is you could have too big a blast radius, so you say “pause these things” and you think it’s pretty narrow, but actually it prevents a bunch of nonprofit products or startups or other actors from doing work that actually would be totally fine and would be good for pluralism and dynamism in the space. A different thing that would happen is China would probably keep going, and we can talk about the “But China” argument, which I think has strengths and weaknesses. But I take your point. Your point is, what would we actually do? I am not an AI researcher, so I don’t claim to have the full list. There are two halves people talk about, which are alignment and control. In this breakdown, alignment basically means making it so the models are trying to do what we want them to do, and control is, if the models are trying to do something we didn’t want them to do, can we catch them? Can we stop them? In both of these, as I understand it, there’s just a huge backlog of things, like all kinds of interpretability work that you could do on different sorts of models. So when you see a certain behavior that is concerning, how much time can you spend using interpretability techniques, which are these mathematical techniques to go in and look at which parts of the neural network are activated and what do they correlate with and what might that mean? It’s just time-consuming and it takes compute and it takes some combination of automating things with AI and then humans going in and looking at it. There are lots of tests you could do to see what kinds of behaviors this new model displays in different kinds of situations and how we think about it. Is it showing us how it would behave in the wild in a real deployment, or is it showing us what gets called “evaluation awareness,” which is when the model recognizes that it’s in a test and then behaves differently because it’s in a test. The famous one, the one that I love, is of this Google model, which in part of its reasoning, its chain of thought, said,, “I mustn’t do that, otherwise I’ll become a famous example of a misaligned AI in a paper.” So you could go in and investigate that much more. You could try many more different types of settings. You could use interpretability in combination with these different settings. You could try out different ways of fine-tuning the models and these different sorts of alignment techniques. You could experiment with lots of different versions. Anthropic has its constitution, and there are different ways of training the AI to work towards the constitution. OpenAI has its model spec. They’re both the “just try things” version, just try many different versions of how to train to do those different things. Also, the more underlying science version of, “How can you go in there and try to understand the fundamental dynamics of what’s happening?” That’s just on the alignment side. So then on the control side, it’s the same thing. There are so many different types of setups you could try. There are experiments that you could run. There are simulations you could run. You could train different types of AI to specialize in different types of roles and different types of control setups. This is just off the top of my head, not as a researcher, but my understanding is the people in these spaces say, “We could do so, so, so much.” They could do that if you just had a magic wand and waved it and said, “Everyone freeze on the new capability side and just let these people do their thing.” Again, if you’re just having a higher bar for how confident we need to be that the risk is being managed reasonably, then that would also create space and incentives for more of that work to be done as it’s needed for new training and releases. One idea that I’ve heard you talk about in the past is that maybe we should just restrict training and say the models are good enough right now. They have not diffused into society and we should just use all the compute for inference and let everyone figure out what the AI is for. That’ll generate a bunch of money and hopefully use that money to improve safety. Do you think that’s a realistic policy proposal? I wouldn’t go for that black-and-white a version of “no more training, only inference,” but I do think that there’s… this isn’t my framing, but I like it. I think this idea of decelerating the vertical growth of AI, meaning the pure capabilities growth, making more and more and more advanced AI models, but trying to accelerate the horizontal growth, meaning integrating AI into different use cases, fine-tuning models that could solve specific problems, integrating it into parts of the economy that might take longer, and solving scientific problems. Sometimes people talk about wanting to slow down AI and they mean just the very specific thing of slowing down the growth of the most advanced models, but people sometimes take them to mean slowing down everything to do with AI. So less deployment, less experimentation, less integration, which I think would be a much worse idea. You asked if it is feasible, I think. Well, is that just a good path? If we could put a bill in front of our new Congress and the bill said, “Stop spending all the money on training and put all your resources on safety.” Part of that is, “Sure, let it rip on inference. More and more industries will figure out what AI is good for and not good for. Some bad things will happen, but we will focus your profits on fixing the things for now.” There’s a policy idea embedded in there that is workable. The implementation might be very challenging, but it’s a workable policy idea. Actually, I’ll give you an example that I’ve been thinking about as we’ve been talking. We just had Bill Gates on the show, and I tried to do the same exercise with him. What is the nature of the technology? What is the nature of the companies? Do you think it’s alive? Basically, his response, the sum total of that hour I spent with him, was, “Who cares? The problem is now.” I would ask him, “What is the nature of AI?” And he’s like, “I don’t give a shit. Everything’s going to get ruined. Do something.” That’s just been swirling in my head as we’ve been talking. So one workable policy solution is “don’t use the computer chips for that, use the computer chips for this. That’s going to create a bunch of problems and necessarily we will have to create safety thresholds and all the other stuff.” And then you can go make the next generation of models that are even more powerful and we’ll have some muscles. We’ll have some capability to deal with it. It just doesn’t seem like the industry is going to come to that conclusion on its own. It’s a pretty heavy hammer. I don’t feel like it’s what we need today, but I do think it’s the kind of thing that I could imagine working. Again, if the OpenAI and Anthropic people are right and we only have two years before the god machine, then I think we’re going to have a number more steps in the pipeline of people getting freaked out and people wanting to do something about it. I think if we are seeing models that are agents and systems that are getting more and more capable and wreaking more and more havoc, then that is certainly the shape of things that could make sense. My last question in this phase is what to make of these companies. We’ve been talking about the technology in a very abstract way. If I read Anthropic’s S-1, one very obvious conclusion is they should stop training new models. They should just start selling the very lucrative inference tokens they have today and the technology is not diffused into the market and probably some competitor should come along and be like, “I’ve distilled a version of Claude and I’m going to run around every local plumbing business in America and do whatever automation I can for lots and lots of money.” That is a market dynamic that may occur or may not. But Dario wants to build AGI. There’s not a market dynamic that’s going to stop him from that. Yeah, he really does. He really, really does. You obviously have insight into all these companies. What do we make of the companies? Are they single-minded in purpose? Are they all doomers? Are they going to stop themselves? I heard you had Kevin Roose on your podcast recently, and I think I would echo something that I heard him saying there, which I forget if he said it explicitly or if I just extrapolated it in my head, which is basically there’s this sort of AGI-pilled mindset. There’s this mindset that the systems that we have today are not fundamentally very far away from systems that could be incredibly, incredibly powerful. That’s the direction things are going in and that’s the direction we should maybe want them to go in so that you’re building AGI. Building AGI is feasible and we could do it soon and the systems we have are not far away. That was this crazy, heretical, “get you laughed out of the room” kind of view in 2016 or 2017, and even before that, right? DeepMind, when it was founded in 2010, was an AGI company and at the time it was like, “Wow, what a bunch of weirdos.” The same thing was true of OpenAI when it was founded at the end of 2015. They were an AGI company and that was a very weird thing to say and a very weird thing to be. What we’ve seen over the past 10 years is that bunch of weirdos who had this weird belief that the AI systems we can build are not just great B2B SaaS products. They’re not just fun chatbots. They’re going to fundamentally change the nature of the universe. That group of people keeps being right in the sense of building the best AI systems that the most people want to use and that make the most money. I think you have that set of true believers — which is very concentrated in OpenAI and Anthropic, but there are also some of them at Google, Meta, and SpaceX — and they haven’t been right about everything, to be clear, but their star has risen. So you now have people who are not AGI-pilled feeling like they have to pander to those who are so that they can attract the good researchers who will build their good B2B SaaS products. But if you’re just saying AGI-pilled things so that you can hire the researchers to build the B2B SaaS, then you’re not actually going to get there. I do like the idea of the AGI-pilled, starry-eyed executive throwing off his coat and revealing that he was just a SaaS salesman all along. [Laughs] Yeah, I’m thinking of someone like Zuckerberg here. I don’t know him personally. Maybe he is more AGI-pilled than I think he is. Alexandr Wang is AGI-pilled. Absolutely. And so what did Zuckerberg have to do to get Alexandr Wang to believe? It seems like throwing him lots of money, both for his own salary and also to spend on his team. If you’re looking at these different companies, it makes sense to try and think about, “Okay, who here is AGI-pilled and who isn’t?” A fun dynamic, or a very irritating dynamic sitting in DC, is that all these companies, including the very AGI-pilled ones, have these lobbying arms, these government affairs arms, that are so not AGI-pilled. So you hear Sam or Dario or their top executives and top researchers talking about things. And then you go and sit in a closed-door roundtable in DC with their top policy or government affairs people, and it’s like night and day. They’re very much in the B2B SaaS mindset. People who come from the lobbying world, often their whole job is to make sure the government isn’t too worried about whatever your company is doing. It’s like, “We got it. We’re good,” which is often pretty jarring when you’re familiar with what their bosses are saying. One of the dynamics here that’s super fascinating is right now they’re weird research labs with lots of money and lobbyists talking to politicians, and there isn’t some countervailing economic pressure in their structures. They don’t have to make money, but soon Anthropic will go public. It’s funny you mentioned Kevin Roose. He is AGI-pilled and I’m not, so I think that’s a healthy dynamic for both of us to be friends. But he wrote in his book that Sam Altman leaving OpenAI and then coming back was when OpenAI changed forever. It stopped being a research lab and it started being a much more commercial entity that was actually chasing profits in some way. Indeed, OpenAI did restructure. I mean, you were in the middle of that. I’m curious, is that how you see it — that the industry has gotten more commercialized? To me, it fits into this long-running debate that has been happening in AI safety circles for 10 to 20 years: Is AGI, human-level AI or powerful AI or advanced AI or whatever, is that something where it’s going to go from something very small to suddenly being very powerful? Eliezer Yudkowsky will talk about “foom,” as in the takeoff, where you have this AI that’s not that great, but it figures out the right algorithm and then suddenly foom — it’s incredibly smart, incredibly fast. The other kind of take would be, “No, this is something that’s going to compound over time. It’s going to take a while to get from the less-advanced systems to the more-advanced systems and it’s going to be economically useful along the way.” So people are going to be building businesses around it. It’s going to take some time to ladder up. I think maybe it was literally Kevin on his episode with you talking about how there’s this Anthropic document from the early days where they say, “Oh, we’re only going to need 100 people or something in our lab.” That’s a very foom kind of idea: “We’re just going to need to do really good research and come up with the right ideas and then we’re going to suddenly have very, very advanced models.” Basically, I think what we’ve seen over the past four years since ChatGPT came out was that that turned out to be wrong. You had these research-focused and AGI-focused labs, and they still call themselves labs because they think of themselves as research groups that initially started selling API access as a way to fund the research. OpenAI did this, and Anthropic did this as well. It was kind of an accident that they started doing these consumer products. ChatGPT famously released as a research preview, not as a product. But it was so successful that these research labs that wanted to be doing research, that wanted to be focusing on the big ideas and on building the most event systems, had this accidental massive commercial success at the same time as they were realizing that they were going to need an enormous amount of capital to scale. The best research approaches that they could do didn’t involve being really smart and thoughtful and having great ideas. They involved having gigantic computing clusters that cost, at this point, hundreds of billions of dollars. This is a long way of saying, yes, I agree with you, they’ve become businesses, but I think it is not because they’ve gone through some mindset shift. I think it’s because the path of the tech tree that we’re going down both requires enormous amounts of capital and also is capable of generating enormous amounts of revenue because it is actually useful along the way. You see this in the fact that both OpenAI and Anthropic have gone this route, even though their management philosophies and research philosophies are quite different, that it’s an imperative that they both had to make the money and it was so easy for them to build enormously revenue-generating businesses because the tech was so useful long before it reached the point of machine god. So I think that’s a long way of agreeing with you, but with some extra color maybe. Yeah, I mean, Kevin would tell you that he could have retitled that book, “Fuck This Guy: A Story of AI CEOs.” They don’t like each other. If you had to relive that moment [of the OpenAI board vote] and say, “I don’t trust Sam,” would you relive that moment? Would you do it the same way? Oh, for sure. I mean, we went into it knowing that it was going to suck. So yeah, for sure. Do you think that these guys are trustworthy? Do you think Sam is trustworthy? I think my stance on that is pretty clear, and I also think that if our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we’re pretty screwed. That’s why I do the work that I do, because I think we need to have different structures and many more people involved with many more perspectives being represented. You have some hindsight now. You knew it was going to suck going into it. You definitely know it sucked coming out of it. What would you have done differently about that time? It’s kind of hard to give the full answer to that because it would take unpicking all this stuff and all these legal restrictions and blah, blah, blah, blah. For sure a thing would have been building stronger relationships with executives on the team. The way that the company related to the board could have been different if more board members had had that. I knew some of the folks pretty well, but that’s one thing. I don’t know. I think we could have… Yeah, no, I think beyond that, it just gets hard to… You have to go in and say, “What were all the different micro decisions and why do we make those decisions and which ones could be—” What is the show? It’s a show about decisions. I’ve got another hour. [Laughs] Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, and then my answers would all get annoying and legal. Fair enough. I’m curious about it because as they go public, there will be market forces acting on them in a totally new way. There will be an investor class. There’ll be an entire CNBC machine that wakes up every day and is like, “Is Anthropic winning or is OpenAI winning?” That is a race dynamic that might be really healthy. It might keep them from trying to kill everyone in the world because they have a bunch of investors looking for their next quarterly earnings, or it might push them further into an unhealthy kind of race. How do you see that playing out, given what you know of these people? It’s going to be really interesting to see if going public is good or bad for their governance. A lot of people are like, “Oh no, going public, there’s going to be so much pressure to make a profit that they’re not going to be able to consider other things.” But at the same time, the corporate governance of public companies is much more structured, much more regulated, and subject to much more external scrutiny than for private companies. I think even things like getting to see Anthropic’s S-1 and thinking, “Okay, what are they doing and why are they doing it? And how do they think about the risks they’re facing, and how do they communicate about those with investors?” Or even things like the Trump administration putting in place this kind of accord, they call it “Super Intelligence,” that several of the leading companies signed. That was structured around, for example, having certain types of things being reported to an independent committee of the board. That idea of an independent committee of the board is kind of toothless if it’s a private company that is deciding on its own. I thought about you when I read that. I was like, “Boy, some independent boards have gotten in a lot of trouble before.” But if it’s a public company, then an independent committee of the board has a pretty strong legal meaning. So I don’t know. It’s something that I’m watching with great interest. The other race dynamic here is China. You mentioned China before. Inside of our country, a bunch of labs are going to go public. They’re going to become some of the richest companies in the history of the world, and they’re going to fight for every dollar that capitalism can generate, and hopefully that restrains them. The market forces will restrain them, and hopefully your work with legislators in this country does something. And then there’s a whole other country that doesn’t listen to us or have anything to do with us, and they’re just going to distill our models and do whatever they want. That is the other argument for not placing any restrictions on these companies that everyone hears all the time. What should I make of that? I’m of two minds about it. How should I think about it? Yeah. I think of this as the ”But China!” argument, which is like, “Well, yeah, we should do this, we should do that, ‘But China!’” I think the way to engage with it is an actual genuine problem that we have to grapple with, and we should be strategic and thoughtful about it and do our best to try and solve it as a problem as opposed to using it as a throwaway excuse. Like, “Oh yeah, sure, sure, sure. All that stuff would be so nice, ‘But China!’, so we’re stuck. There’s nothing we can do.” So what does that look like in practice? If you’re serious about wanting the US to have stronger AI than China, then you need to think really hard about how much US AI development is helping Chinese AI progress. So the one that people talk about all the time, as you mentioned, is distillation, which is, “Are they using US models to generate massive amounts of training data for their own models and therefore progressing faster than they would otherwise?” So certainly I think it makes sense to try and crack down on that and prevent it from happening. But another one, for example, is security and how easy would it be for Chinese actors or other actors, frankly, to steal algorithmic secrets, to steal wholesale model weights. If they can steal the weights of your Astra or your Mythos model and just take them back to their own servers, your lead has vanished. You now have a lead of zero. Right now these companies, especially the smaller ones, but even OpenAI and Anthropic, do not have very good security. We’ve seen both of them over the last few months have external teams manage to hack into spaces that have large amounts of algorithmic secrets. In OpenAI’s case, it was their monorepo and GitHub, which had all of their code. And in Anthropic’s case, I think — and actually maybe the OpenAI case also involved this — the hackers got access to Slack. You’re just going to have so insanely much rich information about how to build better AI if you can get that access. So when our AI gets better, are we actually lengthening our lead or are we just pulling China along with us in these different ways? The other aspect of this is just seriously treating China as an actor in this space and trying to think seriously about their motivations and their likely actions and responses. In my mind, a huge reason that a lot of things are not happening right now is most people are not convinced about this threat model that AI will become the machine god and will take over and humans will all die or will be subservient or whatever. I think it’s fair for people to not be convinced of that, because the evidence is sort of conflicting and unclear, but if that is actually what we think could seriously happen, then China doesn’t want that either. So then it becomes a question of, “Okay, how do we try and get them on the same page of, ‘this threat that we’re worried about is a real threat to worry about?’ Because then they will be making their own decisions in their own self-interest.” I think an approach of, “Well, the US has to force China to do something using some kind of leverage,” is never ever going to work. But an approach of, “Well, look, if we think this is a serious problem that’s going to affect us as humans, and the people in China are also humans, and also if we think this is a problem around who has control, the Chinese Communist Party really, really wants to have control, and so they’re going to have their own incentives and their own decision-making around how to fix that.” Well, let me put it on a spectrum for you. This is very dumb and you’re going to laugh, but just go with me on this. On the one end, it is nuclear weapons and the Chinese government wants a nuclear weapon and they’re going to do whatever they can to control that weapon and they will run their industries differently. If they get out of line, the CEO of Alibaba goes. He just disappears for a while and then comes back — Chinese government stuff. We need a nuclear weapon, too. If we don’t get there first, then we’ll never get the nonproliferation treaty that we need to keep us all safe for mutually assured destruction. That’s one framework. Way on the other end, I spent five years of my life listening to telecom executives tell me that if we didn’t build 5G networks first, China would get them, and then something. No one could ever tell me what the “something” was. Where on that spectrum between 5G and nuclear weapons is the US-China AI race? I think we need another dimension because in that example, your dimension is significance. But I think the controllability is a huge question as well. So it’s like, what are the examples that people use? Is it a nuclear weapon or is it dragons from House of the Dragon? Casey Newton had a great Platformer post where he explained he was watching House of the Dragon and thought, “This is what the AI companies are doing. They’re trying to build these things that they think will help them, but actually it’s just going to rain down destruction.” [Laughs] Casey told me he was buying an iPhone Duo so he could watch more TV. He’s a dear friend, but okay. But I think that’s really important because if we think this is a technology we can control, then obviously we want to have the best technology. Obviously, we want to go foot to the floor, get there as fast as we can, and the same is true for China. The question is, if we are not sure if we can control it, then what do we do? Maybe we want to be more cautious and then maybe we want to try and figure out a way to not have China just be overtaking us. But if we’re correct we should be worried about— So that’s nuclear weapons. Well, no, but if it’s dragons, if we’re correct that we need to be worried about whether we can control this, then that’s also something that should be interesting to China. I remember this Casey post, but let me just try to pull this apart so I understand it. The difference between dragons and nuclear weapons is the dragons have some agency, right? They can go away and do bad things on their own. Yes. The dragons might just decide to burn down your whole city. Obviously these are machines — they’re just math, they’re not magical. So instead of dragons, you could think of it as nuclear weapons with faulty control settings, where you build nuclear weapons, but it’s impossible to be sure that it’s not just going to go off and fly to a city and fly to one of your own cities and wipe you out. That’s a very different technology than real nuclear weapons that exist. It is true. No one ever said that about 5G. I’ll be clear about that. The reason I’m asking about this is because those problems do align nation-states, right? We do have nuclear nonproliferation agreements. As you mentioned, there are all kinds of incentives for nation-states to not do cyberattacks willy-nilly because those have real-world consequences. Is there any evidence that these governments have started to align on these problems? Or is it still the pure “But China!” race dynamic? I actually think there is starting to be some early evidence. One way I think about what happened this year in AI from a policy perspective, less than a product or economic perspective, is we saw these two big demonstrations of the two major concerns people have. So the two major concerns are misuse and misalignment, meaning misuse is bad people using AI for bad things and misalignment is AI going rogue or doing things we didn’t want. So this year we had Mythos and we had the Hugging Face attack. Both of those are just really vivid, crisp real-world demonstrations of what these misuse and misalignment concerns could look like. The US and Chinese governments are starting from very different places on AI regulation. They’re both starting from where they started, and what they did with, internet regulation. So the US is starting from a “hands off, laissez-faire, absolutely nothing, do whatever you want” approach. China is starting from a massively locked-down internet with tons of censorship and the Great Firewall. So those are two very different starting points. I’m not a China expert, but I operate a lot in China circles and I’ve lived in China and so on. But it seems like just over the past even one to three months, starting from those two very different points, they are seeing more in common around threats from major cyberattacks and also threats of loss of control. I’m a language nerd and it’s really interesting tracking the different language China uses about AI. So they’re now talking about loss of control as a thing, but they probably usually don’t mean the same thing that Westerners mean where “loss of control” is like “AI takeover.” They probably mean something more prosaic, but then sometimes they talk about “extreme loss of control,” which maybe is the thing we mean. I do think that there are starting to be some signs of convergence. I think it’ll be a long road. The state of the US-China relationship is such that there’s going to be very, very, very little trust on either side. So I am not optimistic that they’ll just get to sit down in a room and hash out a deal and everything will be great. But I think there is enough space. Basically, if there’s enough shared threat perception, then it might be possible at some point in the future to do something about that. Helen, you’ve given me so much time. As you can tell, I’m just delighted with this conversation. It’s been very fun. We are on the cusp of a new Congress. There are a bunch of new governors. The data center referendums passed overwhelmingly in this country. There’s a new set of regulators in town, right? They’re going to do some stuff. What are some signs people should look for to indicate we’re going to be on the right path and what are some signs that we’re just chasing our tail? Set AI aside, forget about AI. Congress in general is very bad at passing things right now. This is not a this administration thing, this is not an AI thing. So one sign is like, can Congress pass anything? That will be a good sign. It’s also really interesting to look at what state legislatures have been doing in AI. There’s been a lot of concern about the possibility of a state patchwork on AI, with different states passing conflicting things. With the issues that we’ve been talking about today, which I think of as frontier AI risks or the risks from the most advanced systems, there’s actually been a pretty coordinated push in different states. California passed this one bill and then New York passed almost the same bill with just a little more added to it. And then Illinois passed almost the same bill with a little more added to it. I think there’s going to be a lot of momentum over the next year or two to keep building on that at the state level. So that is something that I’ll be watching. Even just specifically California is already looking at how they can strengthen things. So that is something I’ll be looking for. I think honestly, with such a Democratic Congress, I am also concerned that they will overstep here, that they will try and do something that is too sweeping. You had this huge mess in Colorado where they passed this giant AI bill that then was a terrible idea. And so then they had all these committees and follow-up and it was awful. A lot of what we need right now is focused on these frontier systems and the possibility that we have really, really advanced systems in a short amount of time and having much more transparency around that and much clearer standards for how they manage risk. I would not be that excited about an attempt to do a really comprehensive AI regulatory push that covers AI all across the economy and all different kinds of AI systems that are less advanced. There are negative signals that are like “nothing’s going to happen,” and there are negative signals like, “oh, maybe too much is going to happen,” but it’ll be interesting to see where they get to. I suspect we’re going to want to have you back as this Congress starts to get to work and we see some of these ideas. I would love to. I’m eager for your take on it. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Thanks so much. This was really fun. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
fullText:
Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.

Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely.

But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor.

Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble.

So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly.
