title: Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air will be able to control Android XR glasses with gestures
snippet: Android XR glasses get their own control wearable, but you might already own it. Google says the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch will be able to control Android XR glasses. more…
fullText:
Android XR glasses get their own control wearable, but you might already own it. Google says the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch will be able to control Android XR glasses.

Google just launched its line of Intelligent Eyewear glasses. The smart glasses run on Android XR with hardware built by Samsung. They start at $395, with pre-orders opening up today through both Warby Parker and Gentle Monster.

For all the smart features they have, one of the best might be the sly integration Google is setting up between Intelligent Eyewear and its existing wearables. Google quietly noted that both Pixel Watch models and the Fitbit Air will be able to control Android XR glasses, like a dedicated control band some competitor smart glasses come with.

Pixel Watch already supports gesture controls using sensors to detect movements like finger pinching or wrist adjustments. Google’s Android XR demo included pausing and playing music using a pinch gesture. We imagine gesture controls will support as much as the touchpad that sits in the arms of Intelligent Eyewear models, though it’s not clear what gestures will be supported just yet. You’ll still be able to use the touch sensors, but Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air will be just another avenue. 

	

According to what Google told us, the Pixel Watch will be supported around launch, with Fitbit Air adding support sometime in 2027. Galaxy Watch will also be supported on Samsung devices. Considering the Fitbit Air is reportedly such a massive hit that Google is having a hard time keeping up, the move only makes sense. The Fitbit Air is also only $99, whereas something like Meta’s Neural Band goes for $199.

title: I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone
snippet: In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans. more…
fullText:
In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

One of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

The app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

	

You’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned). 

Across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing users. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot. 

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.

title: Google Wallet rolling out digital Google Home keys with supported locks on Android
snippet: Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home. more…
fullText:
Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home.

After adding a home key to Google Wallet, you can Tap to Unlock with your phone. This leverages NFC and “works even when your phone screen is locked” by default. However, you can adjust verification settings in the Google Wallet app to require screen lock or biometric authentication. This requires Android 9+.

There’s also support for Unlock on Approach with an Aliro Ultra Wideband (UWB)-compatible Android phone (see below) and an Aliro UWB-compatible lock. Wear OS watches are not supported at launch.

Google Pixel 10 Pro series and above

Select UWB-enabled Samsung Galaxy phones

Behind the scenes, the digital key is linked to the Google Home app rather than a single lock. As such, “each of your compatible Aliro locks will work with a single key in your Google Wallet.” Keys are added to Google Wallet using the Home app, which will prompt you to save after setup. You can also go to Home settings > Google Wallet key.

	
	

Afterward, your key “automatically syncs across compatible Android phones signed into your Google Wallet account.”

The card in Google Wallet features a simple Google Home logo with your home’s name in the top-right corner. 

The following locks are supported at launch: Aqara u400 (UWB and NFC), Schlage Sense Pro (NFC at launch and UWB to follow), and Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Support for more models is coming.

Additionally, support is rolling out first to the Google Home Public Preview before coming to all users “over the coming weeks.”

Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)

The Drop

The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2. A very simple box that helps you add devices to your smart home (with particular emphasis on music gear), which also kind of acts as a universal controller for all the Bluetooth devices and dumb appliances in your house. Nothing you couldn’t build yourself, but much easier than doing so.

We Chose to Go to the Moon. I was blown away by this live history of the Space Race, complemented by great music and beautiful visuals. Such a cool way to present a story like this, and kept me hooked the whole two hours. I would have watched a bunch more.

TK. A new app from Medium with a bunch of really interesting ideas about how to share your ideas and work with other people without having to do it completely in public. Also just a nice web and mobile app for writing! I’m here for anything that makes people want to blog again.

Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death. From what I’ve seen so far, this is a pretty unsparing look at the horrifying things men are doing to themselves in the name of becoming more attractive. Turns out the story goes back much further than Clavicular, and comes from some pretty bleak places.

Tripod. A lovely new podcast app from Ben Rice McCarthy, who also makes a great camera app and a great social app and is just very good at apps. It has some clever organization features, but it’s also just really well designed, and that is a rare thing to find in a podcast app.

12 12 12. The consensus seems to be that this new Apple TV heist thriller might be too clever by half, but what I’ve seen so far is also just a lot of fun. And at this point? Apple’s track record is good enough that I’ll give almost any new title a few episodes.

Click Through. I am wildly jealous of this podcast idea: Two hosts play The Wikipedia Game, trying to get from one thing to another as fast as possible, narrating and going on tangents the whole way. The first episode is very funny and a very good hang, and I… learned a lot about Greenwich Village?

Google Tabletop. This is just an early prototype of an app, but I love the idea: a collaborative workspace like a Google Doc that can take the form of whatever tool or mini app you need. I immediately have 100 uses for it; I hope Google doesn’t immediately kill it.

The Ring Drone Cam. A drone that can go inspect and see anything in your house: useful! Also terrifying dystopia hellscape! I am desperately curious to know everything about how this $250 gizmo works — though I can tell you confidently my wife will never allow it in our house.

A lot of you out there in the Installerverse have become iPhone Duo users over the last few weeks, and I’ve heard a lot about how you’re all using Apple’s new foldable phone. (I’d say the sentiment in my inbox is roughly 80 percent positive, 5 percent negative, 15 percent deeply confused about interface choices.) I’ve also gotten some questions about which Duo apps are great, and how best to set yours up.

Alas, I do not have a Duo. So I turned to The Verge’s Allison Johnson, who coauthored our review of the device and has used it as aggressively as anyone I know. I asked her to share how she’s wielding the Duo, and she sent over a truly unhinged color scheme and otherwise a bunch of very good ideas. Her’s her homescreen, plus some info on the apps she uses and why:

The phone: iPhone Duo.

The wallpaper: It’s one of those color gradient options you can pick in iOS. I was trying to go for a minimalist thing.

The apps: NYT Games, Kindle, Headspace, Spotify, Google Maps, Safari, Messages, Mail.

So I tried the whole aspirational “dress for the homescreen you want” thing for a few days, with just a few apps like Headspace and NYT Games, and it was a miserable failure. It just made me mad every time I had to search for Messages. I added a row of essential apps to the bottom of the screen and a big calendar widget, and things have been much better.

There’s a big widget / shortcut to TypeDraw, which is a fantastic app on the Duo that makes the whole phone behave like a physical notebook. It’s great with the Apple Pencil. I also realized I need weather close by, so I added a giant widget to the left panel of the homescreen.

I also have a shortcut for the built-in lo-fi playlists on iOS, which is handy if I need to pop in earbuds and play something instrumental so I can focus real quick. Highly recommended to anyone who hasn’t discovered these yet and also gets overstimulated! They’re already on your phone!

I did nuke the dock entirely in my minimalist experiment and I’m actually fine with it. Maybe I’ll never go back to the dock again.

I also asked Allison to share a few things she’s into right now. Here’s what she sent back:

I don’t have a Switch 2 so I’m having extreme Zelda FOMO right now. I WISH I was playing Ocarina of Time but I’m just playing through every last bit of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on my PS5 to distract myself.

I’m like 20 minutes away from finishing Widow’s Bay and that has been a really fun watch.

I just finished reading the Planet Money book, which is like, The Economy For Dummies. It’s pretty entertaining and was very helpful for an economy dummy like me.

I also got a book called Coffee, For Here by an award-winning barista and creator named Morgan Eckroth. They have lots of specialty drink recipes you can make with a home espresso setup. I made one over the weekend and I’m still thinking about how good it was. The photos are beautiful too.

Crowdsourced

Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week.

“Search, a browser developed by a small Parisian design studio of all things. I’d say they have created the classy European cousin of Arc, based on Webkit so it’s super light & responsive on Mac while also having the flexibility of Chrome extensions.” — Elliot

“Trying out Monarch to potentially break my years-long Quicken habit. So far I’m about 90% sure I’m switching.” — Bruce

“Dungeon Crawler Carl. I recently started listening to the audiobook. It has consumed my life. I listen to it on my drive to work, I take breaks at work to listen to it, I play it throughout my day, and eventually fall asleep listening to it. It’s almost 200 hours of content and Jeff Hays does an amazing job voicing all the characters. I’m currently on book seven of eight, and not looking forward to the withdrawals as we wait for book 9. Seriously, check it out.” — William

“Brenpoly on YouTube has open-sourced his “I built an Apple Vision Pro for $5” project. It’s a great watch even if you don’t dabble in 3D printing. It also shows how much potential there is for affordable VR with just the phones in our pockets and some very clever people and communities.” — Owen

“For anyone with an iPhone Duo. On the outer display, Safari keeps a column down the side for its buttons, and web pages stop short of it. I’m a Duo owner, and am now using a great Safari extension called Widen that runs pages underneath that column: ~25% more page, with text kept clear of the buttons.” — Marcus

“I took my kid to see Wildwood, the new Laika movie, this past weekend and left the theater with my jaw on the floor and dragging a few feet behind me. It is extraordinary. For me, put it up there with the all time Studio Ghibli greats. (I know, I know, but I’m serious.) In a way that no Marvel movie special effects have done, I sat at multiple times in the movie thinking, ‘I just can’t believe humans made this.’” — Stephen

“I am a browser snob, constantly flitting back and forth trying to find the one that combines speed with features with proper UX with privacy. I had begrudgingly settled on Safari for Apple and Chrome for everything else when I stumbled upon Brave Origin. It’s a little steep at a one-time purchase of $59, but it’s completely cross platform, syncs, and gets rid of all the Brave cruft. It’s just a good, minimal, fast Chromium-based browser.” — Kait

“Queen’s Domain, a wonderful King’s Field-like game, was released this past weekend and it conjures up all those familiar FromSoftware feelings of combat and exploration! Highly recommended, it’s quite the experience.” — Kyle

“I finished Jet Lag: The Game’s Japanorama, and it is the absolute best tourism video series for Japan without trying at all to be one. It is part scavenger hunt, part race across Japan, and shows off the wonderful scenery and the beautiful public transit of the country. I learnt that Japan loves making lists (OCD folks rejoice!) and has lists of Three Views, Three Great Gardens, 100 Best Sunsets, 100 Remarkable Waters and many more.” — Utkarsh

Signing off

I’m working on a story about the new era of hardware hacking, in which people are suddenly discovering they can vibe-code their way to a better TV, the e-reader of their dreams, and a million other things besides. In almost all my conversations, one thing keeps coming up: the M5Stack developer kits. This company will send you an ESP32-based device you can hack to bits, whether you’re looking for something with an E Ink display or something with a round touchscreen. I’m about to spend an alarming amount of money buying these things, and an equally alarming amount of time making Claude Code do weird stuff with them. I’m already stealing ideas from the fabulous M5Stack subreddit. If you get up to something fun while hardware hacking this weekend, tell me all about it.

See you next week!

title: You can now play Henry Cavill’s ‘Mustache Protocol’ game made on Googlebook [U]
snippet: As teased before the launch, Henry Cavill has built a video game on Googlebook, and it’s called Mustache Protocol. more…
fullText:
As teased before the launch, Henry Cavill has built a video game on Googlebook, and it’s called Mustache Protocol.

Update 11/11: “Mustache Protocol” is now available to play: googlebook.google/henry-cavill.

This 16-bit retro game has three levels and can be played on desktop or mobile. There are “hilarious power-ups and Easter eggs” throughout.

In honor of Movember, your gameplay supports men’s health. From November 11 to 30, for every game played, Google will donate $11 to Movember, up to $500,000. Every play helps drive awareness and funding for men’s mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer.

Original 11/4: Fully embracing the Mission: Impossible – Fallout meme, this 16-bit video game is “about stopping rogue CGI artists from erasing every mustache on the planet.”

	
	

Part of the new platform’s promotional push heading into the holiday season, Google’s announcement says the actor:

“…used Rambler on his Googlebook to organize his thoughts as he brainstormed.”

“…mocked up different aesthetics, added accessories, and fine-tuned the design with Magic Pointer, which let him select and combine visual elements on screen.”

“…was able to move from his Android phone to his Googlebook and back without losing context or interrupting his creative flow” with Continue On

It looks like Cavill used Google Antigravity and other AI tools on the HP Googlebook 14 to “translate natural language prompts into working 16-bit game mechanics.”

The game is not yet available. When it launches, Google will “donate $11 for every play during the month of November” as part of a partnership with Movember. The company will donate up to $500,000 to “help support awareness and funding for men’s mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer.”

Until then, you can watch a three-part series that details how “Henry designed the hero character, vibe coded meme-inspired superpowers, and added to the game’s soundtrack.”

title: End of an era: Apple Support Community forums will permanently close on November 20
snippet: Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details.

If you have ever had a question or ran into a problem with an Apple product, chances are you have come across the Apple Support Community, the company’s official discussion forums where users from around the world help each other troubleshoot issues and share tips.

The platform has a history dating back to at least 1998, when it was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Since then, it was renamed Apple Discussions before relaunching as Apple Support Communities in April 2011, with a redesigned interface, personalized profiles, and a reputation system that rewarded users for helping others.

Tonight, however, users who tried to access the platform were greeted with the following message:

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Right now, the portal still shows a “Sign in” button, though it leads only to an AppleConnect login page labeled “AC Communities Web – Internal,” suggesting that access is now restricted to Apple employees.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

	

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with users able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled new submissions.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and clarification on the scope of the shutdown, and we’ll update this story if we hear back.

(h/t Tim Harbison)

title: Dbrand’s new Fitbit Air band launches as the first official third-party strap
snippet: Dbrand says it was tasked with developing another strap option for the Fitbit Air; thus, the rugged and modern Pulse band was born. more…
fullText:
Dbrand says it was tasked with developing another strap option for the Fitbit Air; thus, the rugged and modern Pulse band was born.

Google has a small collection of official accessory partners it works with to create third-party add-ons for its products under the “Made for Google” umbrella. Dbrand happens to be one of them, and has been since the launch of the Pixel 7.

Available starting today, the Dbrand Pulse band launches for the Fitbit Air starting at $34.95. It’s the first official Made for Google strap that fits the Fitbit Air. It comes in two sizes and one color – black. It’s definitely a more rugged option, but having worn a pre-production unit for a couple of months, I can safely say it’s the most comfortable Fitbit Air band I’ve worn.

It’s constructed of sweat-resistant silicone with molded channels to let air in. It certainly looks like a heavy-duty band, which is perfect for a wearable made to go with you wherever.

	

We’ve expressed our frustrations with Google’s selection of straps before, but this is the first sign of Google looking to other partners to develop more options. Dbrand claims Google tasked them with developing a new band because the Fitbit Air has been such a major success. Hopefully, we see more Made for Google brands release bands for the Fitbit Air. This is a great first step.

Dbrand’s Pulse band for the Fitbit Air is available on the company’s website, starting today.

title: 30% of iPhone Duo buyers may have returned it, but I don’t think Apple should worry
snippet: A poll of 9to5Mac readers who were lucky enough to take delivery of their iPhone Duo in the first few days shows that 30% of them have returned it for a refund. While that could be considered bad news for the future of the device, I don’t personally consider it either surprising or worrying … more…
fullText:
A poll of 9to5Mac readers who were lucky enough to take delivery of their iPhone Duo in the first few days shows that 30% of them have returned it for a refund.

While that could be considered bad news for the future of the device, I don’t personally consider it either surprising or worrying … 

Following a report by The Verge on iPhone Duo buyers who opted to return the device for a refund within Apple’s 14-day “no questions asked” period, we thought it would be interesting to get a sense of how many people may have done this.

9to5Mac readers were always likely to have had their fingers hovering over the pre-order button for the best shot at taking early delivery, with the first of these having hit the end of the 14-day window. We ask those of you who fall into this category to tell us whether you kept or returned the device.

With close to 6,000 total votes, the results showed that close to a third of you returned your Duo.

For any other device, that would be a disastrous return rate. For the Duo, however, I don’t think it’s terribly surprising.

	

As we noted yesterday, Apple described the iPhone Duo as “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original.” The size of that change shows up in a whole range of ways, from the weight of the device through the changed aspect ratio of the front display to a completely new way of using an iPhone. 

Throw in the extremely high price tag, and I’ve always suspected that a significant number of iPhone Duo buyers would be viewing it as an experiment rather than a committed purchase. Our own Ryan Christoffel is an example of that “try it and see” attitude. One week in, he’s reached an interim conclusion that it’s probably not for him.

For those who’ve decided to return it, a number of readers shared their reasons.

“Returned it – I can’t go back to Touch ID.”

“Returned it. Cameras are key for me.”

“I want to like it, but I just can’t get there. It’s awkward, and the outside screen is way too small.”

“Returned it. Not for me. I do not want to open the phone every time I want a larger screen and Apple made the outer display much less usable than it should be with that silly permanent dock. I also use my phones left-handed.”

“During a vacation in Morocco, we spent a night camping in the Sahara Desert. I was extremely careful with the phone and tried to avoid using it in the sand altogether. However, on the second day, when I opened it inside the tent, I heard a crunching sound coming from the hinge. Sand had somehow gotten inside. I tried everything I could to clean it, but nothing worked. The inner display was still functioning perfectly, but the phone would no longer open all the way. Even worse, when I tried to close it, I had to force it shut.”

For me personally, it couldn’t be my only phone, given the priority I place on the device as a camera, but I am still lusting after it. Given the continued extended delivery times – with random checks showing shipping in late January – I don’t think Apple has much to worry about here.

title: AMD Issues Fix for GPU Software Issue That Wore Down SSDs
snippet: AMD released a new version of its Adrenalin Edition graphics software to address excessive SSD writing.
fullText:
AMD issued a software update on Thursday to fix a driver issue that caused excessive, continuous data writes to solid-state drives across its Radeon GPU lineup.

First reported on sites including Tom’s Hardware and Neowin, the bug was traced to two pieces of software: AMD External Events Client Module and Utility, known as atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe under Windows processes. The background service handles monitoring functions, but as some users have noticed, it’s also writing a large amount of data to SSDs, as much as 432GB in 24 hours, according to Neowin.

The optional update is available on AMD’s website as Adrenalin Edition 26.11.1. In the notes for the update, AMD said the new software addresses “excessive system-drive writes while the system is idle on Radeon RX 7000 series graphics products and above” and “excessive system-drive writes while moving or resizing application windows.”

			

More from CNET

This excessive data writing is a concern because it can accelerate the wear and tear on an SSD, potentially shortening its lifespan. According to PC Gamer, that could mean losing 1% of the drive’s health in just a month. As one Reddit poster pointed out, this is not a new bug and, in one case, may have caused SSD degradation for nearly a year and a half.

Company staffers were previously posting on Reddit that a fix was coming. 

The cost of SSDs has spiked dramatically in the last couple of years, so it could be an expensive problem to fix if it causes significant wear on a drive.

How to check for the bug

The same Reddit users who helped uncover the bug and spread the word have a few ideas for how to prevent this if you haven’t updated to the new software. First, check the Windows Resource Monitor (you can access it by pressing Windows key + R and typing “resmon”) and look in the Disk tab to see if you’re experiencing excessive writing to your SSD from either atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe processes.

Some who are seeing this are disabling the External Events software entirely. You can do that in Windows by typing Windows key + R and entering “services.msc.” Once there, you can look for the AMD External Events Utility, open its Properties and set Startup Type to Disabled. That will keep it from starting up automatically when you reboot. You can also stop the process while you’re there for the current session. You’ll want to restart your computer after this change.

Keep in mind that disabling the software could affect some display functions and game performance. Others have tried disabling a Resizable Bar, or ReBAR, a PCI Express process for accessing video card memory. Some have switched to alternative AMD drivers that are only compatible with AMD chipsets, not those with Intel or other chipset motherboards.

These options may be a temporary fix if you’re unable to install the new software, but be warned: Using any of those methods carries the risk of breaking other functions on your machine, so make sure your system has a recent restore point.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Omar Gallaga
						

						

											

								

											Omar Gallaga has covered technology, digital culture and other topics for outlets including CNET, NPR, Wired, Texas Monthly, MSNBC, Consumer Reports, The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, The Atlantic and the Austin American-Statesman, where he was a longtime tech reporter, editor and podcaster. He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s Curtain Track 4 is the easiest smart curtain retrofit yet
snippet: The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge. more…
fullText:
The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track. You hang it on the track between the curtain hooks, run a one-tap calibration in the SwitchBot app, and your existing curtains can then be motorized and used in your smart home. There’s no drilling, no rewiring, and no need to position magnets to stick to the rail, as earlier SwitchBot curtain motors required. SwitchBot claims the whole setup takes about 30 seconds.

One thing to check first: this version is for U-rail tracks only, not curtain rods.

SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 battery

The Battery+ version pairs a small built-in battery with a detachable 5,000mAh module for a total of 6,400mAh. SwitchBot rates it at up to 12 months of use for each charge, depending on curtain weight and movement frequency. When it needs charging, you pull the module off, charge it via USB-C, and clip it back on. SwitchBot also sells a Solar version that uses a small panel to keep the battery topped off if the window gets enough sun.

SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 in Apple Home

The motor itself connects via Bluetooth, so getting it into Apple Home requires a compatible SwitchBot Hub, which brings it there via Matter. Once it’s there, the curtains work like any other window covering in your Home app. You can add them to scenes, control them with Siri, and include multiple windows in a single automation. It’s always nice to time smart curtains/shades with dusk/dawn as well.

SwitchBot’s built-in QuietDrift mode opens the curtains slowly in the morning, at about half a centimeter per second, so the room fills with daylight gradually rather than all at once. SwitchBot says it runs at around 25 dB in that mode. You can also give the curtain a gentle tug by hand and the motor takes over, which is great if you don’t have your iPhone with you or someone doesn’t have access to your Apple Home setup.

SwitchBot built it in a way to correct drift over time, so you shouldn’t need to recalibrate it if it gets off.

Wrap up on SwitchBot Curtain Track 4

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 turns the U-rail curtains you already have into Apple Home window coverings without replacing anything. The detachable battery is the best feature here, as it lets you charge it without a long cord.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is available now on Amazon and directly from SwitchBot.

title: Apple just released new AirPods Pro 3 firmware and more
snippet: Apple is rolling out brand new firmware for select AirPods models today, including AirPods Pro 3. Here are the details on how to update. more…
fullText:
Apple is rolling out brand new firmware for select AirPods models today, including AirPods Pro 3. Here are the details on how to update.

Latest AirPods firmware arrives two months after last update

New AirPods firmware is here, debuting nearly two months after the last noteworthy update.

Today’s new AirPods firmware is build 9B47. The previous build was 9A348, which shipped alongside iOS 27 in September.

The latest firmware is rolling out for H2-equipped AirPods models. Currently it’s only available for select models, but it’s expected to ultimately debut for:

AirPods Pro 3

AirPods Pro 2

AirPods 5

AirPods 4

AirPods Max 2

So far release notes haven’t yet been published, but they’ll be added to this webpage soon. It’s likely the firmware only includes “bug fixes and other improvements,” but we’ll keep you posted if something more substantive materializes.

You can’t manually trigger AirPods firmware installation like you can iPhone software updates. Instead, updates happen automatically in the background. Here are Apple’s official instructions for getting the quickest install:

Make sure that your iPhone, iPad, or Mac is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS, and that Bluetooth is on.

Make sure that your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

title: New Apple TV 4K remote’s best feature requires a newer iPhone model
snippet: A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone. more…
fullText:
A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone.

Precision Finding for new Siri Remote requires iPhone 17 or newer

If you’re interested in the new Apple TV 4K launching this week, or perhaps you just want to buy the upgraded Siri Remote separately (available here), there’s a key limitation you should know.

Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote requires an iPhone 17 or newer.

The most common problem with the current Siri Remote is that it’s easy to lose. And once you lose it, Apple doesn’t offer many options for finding it. But that’s changing with the 4th gen Siri Remote.

You can use the new Siri Remote with any previous Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD model. And if you do, you’ll benefit from the remote’s new built-in speaker that can be triggered from the Find My app.

Joining the new speaker, the other main change with this latest Siri Remote is Precision Finding. If you’ve ever used the Find My app to track down a lost AirTag, you’ll probably be familiar with the feature.

Precision Finding lets you get step-by-step, guided directions that take you directly to the lost Siri Remote. It’s a huge upgrade from the old tool for finding the remote—which mostly just told you that it’s in your house somewhere.

But Precision Finding relies on the Bluetooth 6 support found in iPhone 17 and 17 Pro models (not iPhone 17e), iPhone Air, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 18 Pro models.

So if you don’t have one of those iPhones, you’ll still benefit from the built-in speaker that lets you play a sound to find the lost remote, but Precision Finding won’t be available.

You can buy the new Siri Remote for $59 on Amazon.

title: Galaxy S27 redesign leak shows off Pro vs Ultra size difference, with just a bit of controversy
snippet: Samsung is working on a long overdue redesign for its Galaxy S27 series and, this week, we’re getting a fresh look. more…
fullText:
Samsung is working on a long overdue redesign for its Galaxy S27 series and, this week, we’re getting a fresh look.

We’ve already seen it in renders, but leaker Sonny Dickson took to Twitter/X today to present an image of Galaxy S27 Pro, Ultra, and S27+ dummy units, and it tells us a few things. 

First, we get to see the redesign again, this time in “real life.” That’s, of course, with the caveat that these aren’t real devices, and probably aren’t reflective of the final design either. The Pro and Ultra both have a full-width camera island akin to Apple’s latest iPhone design language, and a big departure from the vertical camera array that Samsung insisted was its “core identity” mere months ago.

Importantly, we can also see the size difference between Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro, with the Pro being noticeably smaller compared to both the Ultra and the S27+. For small(er) phone fans, it’s looking great.

	

All of that said, adding a bit of controversy to this image is leaker Ice Universe, who says “this picture is wrong.”

Ice points out that the Galaxy S27 Ultra and Pro both do not have a fourth camera lens, which is correct based on recent leaks. That said, it’s not much of a leap to assume these dummy units are based on an older design, or are confusing a sensor. After all, these are mainly used to test accessories and, this early on, there’s plenty of room for inaccuracy.

What do you think of this image? Do you think it’ll look like the final product? Do you like the size difference on the Galaxy S27 Pro?

title: I feel a little nostalgic about the Apple Support Community forums, but it was time
snippet: Yesterday brought a surprise move by Apple when it abruptly ceased write access to the Apple Support Community and announced that it would be permanently closing in just over a week. While the news does make me a little nostalgic, I do have to say that I think its time had long since come and gone … more…
fullText:
Yesterday brought a surprise move by Apple when it abruptly ceased write access to the Apple Support Community and announced that it would be permanently closing in just over a week.

While the news does make me a little nostalgic, I do have to say that I think its time had long since come and gone …

As we noted yesterday, the community has a fairly long history. It started in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange before being renamed Apple Discussions and finally relaunching as Apple Support Communities in 2011. There were some paid community specialists working for Apple on the forum, while the majority of the responses came from volunteers.

The company’s statement was brief and didn’t give any official explanation for the shutdown.

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

Interestingly, Verizon did exactly the same thing with its own Community Forum earlier this year, with an immediate switch to read-only access, followed shortly afterwards by closing it altogether. That too had a reasonably long history, having first launched back in 2008.

	

I suspect in both cases this was mostly about streamlining operations and reducing costs. CEO John Ternus does seem to be aiming to improve efficiency and eliminate what he views as unnecessary expenses. Additionally, community forums always run the risk of reputational damage when customers criticize decisions made by the company.

I’m old enough to remember the times when the forum was one of the first places I’d turn when troubleshooting an issue with an Apple product, but in all honesty, that hasn’t been the case for a very long time now. A lot of the suggestions were very basic steps any experienced user would already have tried.

There was sometimes also a snarky tone to some of the responses, essentially amounting to “Apple doesn’t promise you should be able to do X, so why are you expecting to do this?” or “Apple already provides a better way to do Y so use it.”

If you were very new to Apple devices and needed very basic help, then I’m sure it could sometimes prove useful, but I have to say that for a very long time now my own starting point has always been Reddit. I don’t think too many people are going to mourn the passing of ASC.

title: November 2026 Pixel Drop: Create My Widget, HiLight for Google Messages, Pixel 10 Rambler, & more
snippet: Like last year, the next Pixel Drop is rolling out a month early in November. Coupled with Android 17 QPR2, it’s quite a big Feature Drop for Gemini and other AI capabilities, as well as the Pixel 10 series. more…
fullText:
Like last year, the next Pixel Drop is rolling out a month early in November. Coupled with Android 17 QPR2, it’s quite a big Feature Drop for Gemini and other AI capabilities, as well as the Pixel 10 series.

Pixel Watch Drop: Create My Widget, Phone-to-Watch Unlock, and Wear OS 7.1

Gemini Intelligence is coming to the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold. The lead feature is Rambler to automatically remove filler words and format your transcription.

The Pixel 10 series also gets Gemini app automation for ordering groceries, ride-sharing, meal delivery, marketplace transactions, and booking reservations. Proactive Gemini Actions let you “send groceries right to your Google Keep list straight from ongoing conversations” and more.

	

The Pixel 11 and 10 are getting Create My Widget. This generative UI capability lets you create custom homescreen objects using natural language. For example, you can create a sports widget or an event countdown. The feature first debuted on Googlebooks.

On the Pixel 11, Gemini Call Screen is an “intelligent, proactive assistant that screens incoming inquiries on demand.” Replacing Manual Call Screen, Gemini will speak to callers in a more conversational manner than before.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 10+ now lets Gemini make calls on your behalf in the US. Use cases include changing reservations, putting items on hold, and checking inventory. Beta testing started in September.

The AI features continue with 10 new Custom Icon styles. Following the March introduction, Google has upgraded the experience with Nano Banana for higher-quality icons. Available on Pixel 6a+.

Pixel Solver in the Google Calculator app provides generative AI custom templates and allows for conversational, multi-step problem solving using prompts. This is available on Pixel 11+.

Unit Conversion is a “top-tier module” that saves you from switching between your browser and the Calculator app. It offers inline mathematics, combined unit interpretation, and real-time exchange rates on the Pixel 6a+.

On the Pixel 11 Pro, Pro XL, and Pro Fold, HiLight now supports Google Messages notifications after being restricted to phone calls and Gemini at launch. 

Pixel Search is now available on the Pixel 6 and newer to provide a more integrated on-device lookup experience that spans apps, web, settings, and other personal content. It allows for natural language search from the search bar at the top of the app grid. 

	

Extreme Battery Charging is now available on the Pixel 10 series.

Following the 2.0 redesign in September, Pixel VIPs now supports Live Location Sharing. This will surface real-time information and battery status from Find Hub in contact cards and homescreen widgets on the Pixel 6a+. 

Transit Mode has been upgraded to automatically trigger based on device sensors. This is available on the Pixel 6a+.

International feature expansions today include:

Notification Summaries are now available in Germany, Canada, France, Spain, Italy, India, and Taiwan on Pixel 9+.

Similarly, Notification Organizer is now available in German and Japanese.

title: Nintendo Switch 2 emulation on Android already has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake up and running
snippet: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development. more…
fullText:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

	

9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

title: iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day
snippet: iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

#1: Siri AI’s new app actions

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

#2: New Apple Health app

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

#3: Siri Recap

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

title: Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal
snippet: A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details.

A bit of background

In recent years, Apple’s deal with Alphabet to make Google the default search engine on Safari has drawn regulatory attention in the US, the UK, and Australia, while related search competition concerns have also come under scrutiny in the EU and Japan.

While the details of each investigation differ, they all raise concerns about the impact of Google’s dominance in search, as well as the extent to which its agreements with other companies might be limiting competition.

More recently, Apple’s agreement with Google received significant attention during the US Department of Justice’s antitrust case against the search giant, which included testimony from Apple executives Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea. The latter joined Apple from Google in 2018 and led its AI efforts until stepping down earlier this year.

As a result of the US case, a federal judge ruled in August 2024 that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in online search through anticompetitive agreements, including its deal with Apple.

Now, evidence presented during that trial has become central to a class action against Apple in Canada, which a British Columbia Supreme Court judge recently certified.

Canadian class action certified

The case was initially brought in 2021 by Spark Event Rentals Ltd., an event rental company based in British Columbia. The plaintiff alleged that Apple and Google conspired to limit competition in the search market, allowing Google to charge advertisers artificially inflated prices.

Apple, meanwhile, argued that its agreement with Google was a legitimate distribution arrangement rather than an unlawful conspiracy. The company also maintained that Google was the appropriate defendant, describing itself as an “innocent bystander.”

Interestingly, the lawsuit originally named both Apple and Google as defendants, but the plaintiff later dropped Google from the case following a dispute over an arbitration clause in its advertising contracts.

With Apple now the sole defendant, Justice Thomas has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, finding sufficient grounds to examine whether Google’s payments discouraged Apple from developing its own search engine.

The lawsuit seeks financial compensation for advertisers who allegedly overpaid for Google search ads, and the court has also allowed the question of punitive damages to proceed.

The class action covers Canadian residents who purchased search ads from Google since 2005, when Apple and Google first agreed to make Google the default search engine on Safari in exchange for a share of advertising revenue.

Importantly, the ruling does not establish that Apple engaged in anticompetitive conduct, but simply allows the allegations to proceed as a class action.

From the decision:

The central proposition raised by these pleadings is that Apple could have used its resources and distribution network to enter the search engine market, but chose not to because Google paid Apple billions of dollars in revenue-share payments to make Google the default search provider on Apple products. This arrangement gave Google market power, enabling it to charge supracompetitive advertising prices on search engines.

In my view, this pleads a common purpose to perform an act prohibited by s 45 of the Competition Act, such that it is not “clear and obvious” that the plaintiff has not pleaded an agreement between Google and Apple not to compete in the search engine market.

At one point in his decision, Justice Thomas cites Giannandrea’s testimony and directly quotes Cue’s from the US antitrust trial, before concluding that “this provides some basis in fact, supporting the inference that Apple did not compete with Google in the search engine market because of its Agreement with Google.”

Interestingly, the judge also acknowledges Apple’s objections to the evidence, agreeing that “the plaintiff has cherry-picked evidence to support his case,” but adding that, in his view, “it is appropriate to do so at this stage in the proceedings.”

With the class action greenlit, the case can now move forward toward trial, though no date has been announced yet.

title: Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang’s ‘scheme’ with Trump
snippet: This Congressional investigation into Nvidia's China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke.
fullText:
Democrats on Thursday opened an inquiry into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China. Earlier on Thursday, the company ousted its CEO Jensen Huang. He also agreed to testify to a different set of Republican-led Congressional committees.

Huang was removed from the company he founded after he confessed to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. (He has since been accused of having more affairs, with Nvidia employees.)

The alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Democratic inquiry comes from Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. As the minority party, they can ask questions but can’t compel answers.

Their humdinger of a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asks the department to preserve records about an arrangement they find questionable and, they allege, illegal.

“The scheme worked like this,” as the letter describes it. President Trump agreed to sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China as long as the chips, manufactured by Taiwan, were first shipped to the United States. On arriving, Trump added a tariff “effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system,” the letter said. Then the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, issued an export license.

By the way, the deal between Trump and Nvidia to share revenue was public. In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD both agreed to share 15% of their revenue from chip sales to China with the U.S. government as part of a deal to secure export licenses, the AP reported at the time.

But the letter questions why Lutnick continued to allow Megaspeed to buy chips even after he was reportedly informed by U.S. intelligence of their suspicions of Alice Huang and of Jensen Huang’s relationship with her. It questions why the department reportedly green-lit other Asian companies to buy Nvidia chips “with no physical presence at their listed addresses.” So the inquiry is aimed at the administration, not just at Nvidia and Huang.

The letter also questions how Nvidia’s donations to Trump’s projects factored in. It notes that the export deal was approved after Trump learned of “Mr. Huang’s compromised position” in sleeping with an alleged spy, and after Nvidia donated $26 million toward Trump’s projects, including the ballroom. It appears to be asking if Trump used his knowledge of the affair to secure donations from Nvidia.

Interestingly, in a “60 Minutes” interview with President Trump that aired on Sunday, Trump mentioned how he and his team had threatened an unnamed AI exec with jail, and after that, the exec “totally changed.”

This Congressional investigation into Nvidia’s China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke. The Republican-led group involves leaders from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House Intelligence Committee. That group has demanded that Huang come to them and testify in a closed-door session. They had threatened to subpoena him if he didn’t voluntarily agree. On Thursday, after his resignation, he agreed.

title: Put That Pan Anywhere: Miele’s New Induction Cooktop Is One Big Burner
snippet: The unique full-surface cooktop accommodates up to six pieces of cookware at once, anywhere you place them.
fullText:
Miele is expanding its catalog of high-end kitchen appliances with the North American debut of its full-surface induction cooktops, which allow you to move your pots and pans wherever you please across the entire surface of the stove.

While gas ranges were long seen as the reigning champ of stovetops among chefs, induction has slowly but surely won over many professional and home cooks alike thanks to its even heat distribution, eco-friendliness, cleanliness and safety factors. 

Instead of heating the stovetop surface like an electric range or using an open flame like gas, an induction stovetop transfers heat directly to the cookware. As a result, it’s faster and safer than the other two options. Although the surface can still warm from the cookware, it cools faster, reducing the risk of accidental burns.

			

More from CNET

Miele’s previous induction cooktops had designated cooking zones, but now that two full-surface models were introduced in the US, cooks have much more flexibility to move pots around as needed while preparing meals. Miele says it has intelligent pot-recognition technology so the stovetop can instantly detect the position and size of each cooking pot and display the control elements in the right place. If you move your cookware around, the power settings will follow.

	

			

	

			

									

						 Gas vs. Electric vs. Induction: How To Choose The Right Range					

							

		

“I’ve become an induction stovetop evangelist. Air quality was my biggest reason for switching, but they’re also just so darn easy to clean,” CNET’s home and kitchen editor, David Watsky, said. “I’ve run out of cooktop real estate more times than I can count. In theory, you’ll be able to cram as many skillets and saucepans as will fit on Miele’s novel induction cooktop, including oversized cookware, and know every inch is getting heat.”

The Miele cooktops are available in 30- and 36-inch sizes and can fit up to six pieces of cookware at once.

“With framed and frameless options, the new models provide the user with greater choice in how the cooktop integrates into the overall kitchen,” Dirk Sappok, Miele North American Region director of Category Management, Kitchen Appliances, said in a press release.

The digital controls on Miele’s new induction cooktops disappear if cookware is not on the stovetop.Miele

Miele’s 30-inch, full-surface cooktop is available for $6,000, while the 36-inch option is $7,000.

“This is not a budget option — most Miele products aren’t — but if it works as well as advertised, it’ll serve as welcome innovation to the induction stovetop category,” Watsky said. “I can definitely see other brands integrating similar technology in future releases.”

title: CleanupBuddy 2.0 expands beyond the keyboard with new display cleaning features
snippet: Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details.

Useful update with fun tidbits

If you’re not familiar with CleanupBuddy, this is a nice little app that locks the keyboard to prevent accidental inputs while the user cleans it up.

Once they’re done cleaning, users can press and hold both Cmd keys to unlock the keyboard, then proceed to grease it up again.

The app also features a fun little animated character that reacts to your cleaning sessions with playful (and sometimes snarky) comments.

Today, CleanupBuddy was updated to version 2.0, with options to dim the display and ignore touch inputs, making it useful for users of both the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Macs with traditional displays.

From the release notes:

You can use the new “Lock Touch Screen” option to block touch input while cleaning a supported touch screen. On Macs without a touch screen, the “Dim Display” option can still be used to darken the display for easier cleaning.

Today’s update also tweaks the in-app character, which now uses on-device Apple Intelligence to generate personalized comments before and after cleaning sessions, based on stats such as time spent cleaning, key presses, and mouse clicks.

Rambo explains that these stats are collected only during cleaning sessions and stored locally on the Mac, and that users can independently turn off both cleanup stats and Apple Intelligence integration in the app’s settings.

Other tweaks in today’s update include temporarily disabling Sticky Keys and its Shift-key shortcut during cleaning sessions, as well as improving the readability of the “Start Cleanup” button when using Liquid Glass.

CleanupBuddy 2.0 is available for $2.99 and is compatible with macOS 14 and later, while the new personalized messages require macOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled and its models ready to use.

title: iCloud+ has new perk in iOS 27 if you pay for more storage
snippet: The tentpole feature of iCloud+ is cloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding the service to include other perks too. And in iOS 27, iCloud+ has a new benefit for high-storage tiers: AI features for HomeKit cameras. more…
fullText:
The tentpole feature of iCloud+ is cloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding the service to include other perks too. And in iOS 27, iCloud+ has a new benefit for high-storage tiers: AI features for HomeKit cameras.

iCloud+ now includes AI features for HomeKit cameras on 2TB, 6TB, 12TB plans

With iOS 27, iCloud+ has added a new perk if you pay for more storage: Apple Intelligence features for compatible Home cameras. Per Apple’s website:

With Apple Intelligence in the Home app, you can automatically generate video descriptions for recorded clips from compatible Home cameras. You can then search your recordings using natural language

These AI-generated video descriptions provide a convenient summary of what’s happening in your home, let you browse important clips at a glance, and search the camera’s recent history of recordings.

	

All of this is available with a camera that supports HomeKit Secure Video (I recommend this Aqara camera for $35). But because AI features depend on Private Cloud Compute, Apple only offers them on the following iCloud+ plans:

2TB plan: up to 1 camera

6TB plan: up to 2 cameras

12TB plan: up to 5 cameras

Apple charges $9.99, $29.99, and $59.99/month for each of these plans, respectively. So most users probably won’t find the monthly cost worth it for AI camera features alone. But if you already need a lot of iCloud storage, now you’ll get these new features thrown in too.

Note: these AI features have additional requirements too. You’ll need a home hub like a HomeView, Apple TV 4K, or HomePod, and your iPhone must support Apple Intelligence.

title: Google Gemini for CarPlay now available
snippet: Google’s Gemini AI chatbot app for Apple CarPlay is now available. The company confirmed that it is bringing the full Gemini Live conversation experience to CarPlay on Wednesday, and the app update arrived on Thursday. more…
fullText:
Google’s Gemini AI chatbot app for Apple CarPlay is now available. The company confirmed that it is bringing the full Gemini Live conversation experience to CarPlay on Wednesday, and the app update arrived on Thursday.

CarPlay now supports every major AI chatbot 

Google bringing Gemini to CarPlay is especially notable for one reason. Gemini was the last major AI chatbot holdout.

CarPlay has supported AI chatbot apps and other conversational apps for a while now.

iPhone apps including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Copilot, Meta AI, and Grok all shipped CarPlay support already. Siri includes a standalone app in iOS 27, which also supports CarPlay.

Google has previously supported Gemini features through Google Maps on CarPlay, but not the Gemini Live experience through the dedicated chatbot app. 

Gemini CarPlay app is out now

“Gemini on Apple CarPlay is rolling out globally starting today to all Gemini users on iOS across every supported Gemini Live language,” Google says.

“To get started, make sure you’ve updated to the latest version of the Gemini app on your iPhone, enabled microphone permissions, and used Gemini Live on your phone at least once. The next time you connect your phone to your car, tap the Gemini icon on your CarPlay display, then start a new conversation or pick up a recent one.”

Google Gemini for CarPlay is now available through the iPhone App Store.

title: Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands
snippet: Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples. more…
fullText:
Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm. 

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

	

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.” 

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Booklight is also on the Play Store.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google. 

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

title: ‘Hey Gemini’ hotword debuts on Android XR glasses
snippet: Google is finally introducing a “Hey Gemini” hotword for its AI assistant, but it’s only on Android XR glasses to start. more…
fullText:
Google is finally introducing a “Hey Gemini” hotword for its AI assistant, but it’s only on Android XR glasses to start.

Around a decade after “Hey Google” made its debut, Google is introducing its first new always-listening hotword. “Hey Gemini” makes its debut on Google’s Intelligent Eyewear glasses powered by Android XR, with wearers able to use that hotword in place of “Hey Google.”

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

This is a move that doesn’t come as a huge surprise. If anything, it’s perhaps a bit overdue.

The move from Assistant to Gemini would have been the expected place for Google to make this change, but it’s one that many will certainly welcome. While the hotword you use really won’t matter much at the end of the day, “Hey Google” has been recognized by many to not roll of the tongue very nicely. It’s a phrase that’s easy to stumble over, where “Hey Gemini” is a bit smoother. 

	

As for whether or not “Hey Gemini” will become the default on future product remains unclear, but it’s a change only available on glasses for now.

We’ve asked Google if both hotwords will be active on Android XR glasses, but it was implied that this is, in fact, the case. When paired to Samsung glasses, “Hey Bixby” may also be in play, as Samsung’s voice assistant is supported on Intelligent Eyewear. Exact functionality, though, is something we’re still waiting for more clarity on.

fullText:

snippet: After being barebones at launch, Google is improving on Pixel 11 Pro’s Hilight feature with message support, now including WhatsApp. more…
fullText:

title: Android Auto 18.2 update starts rolling out with more light mode teases
snippet: Google has started rolling out the Android Auto 18.2 update, but don’t expect much to change on your car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google has started rolling out the Android Auto 18.2 update, but don’t expect much to change on your car’s display.

Heading first to beta users, Android Auto 18.2 has started rolling out. This comes a little over a week after Android 18.1 hit the stable release track.

As Android Auto users should be very used to at this point, the update itself doesn’t bring any new user-facing changes that we can see. That’s not to say nothing is changing. There’s an endless list of bugs Google can fix. Just a few recent examples include Gemini bugs, foldable headaches, strange UI issues, connection problems, double-skipping songs, and more. Bug fixes are the primary point of these smaller Android Auto app updates.

Notably, this update also doesn’t fully cut off users on older Android versions yet. Google has confirmed Android 11 will be the new minimum requirement, but Android Auto 18.2 still supports as far back as Android 9.

	

Now, what about behind the scenes?

About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.

Our teardown of Android Auto 18.2 didn’t turn up much of interest.

The biggest noteworthy change is that Google has updated over 100 assets within the Android Auto app in preparation of light mode support. These are largely around various button designs in the experience, such as:

res/drawable/ic_mr_button_connected_14_dark.xml

res/drawable/ic_mr_button_connected_15_dark.xml

Light mode for Android Auto is something we’ve been waiting ages to see go live, and every recent update has been building out the feature more and more. As for when it will be released, that’s anyone’s guess.
